image_caption: Korean woodblock print of the Platform Sutra

title: Record of Linji (Linji lu)
creator: linji
location: Zhenzhou, Hebei; edited at Gushan, Fujian
note: The sermons, dialogues and deeds of Linji Yixuan, the most famous Chan 'recorded sayings' text, with its call to 'kill the Buddha' if you meet him.
description: Compiled by his disciple Sansheng Huiran and re-edited by Yuanjue Zongyan in 1120, the Record of Linji gathers his public sermons, encounters with students and colleagues, and an account of his training under Huangbo. Linji urges his hearers to stop seeking outside themselves and to recognise the 'true person of no rank' who is present in their seeing and hearing; to break attachment he speaks of slaying buddhas and patriarchs and uses shouts and blows. Scholars note that the text grew with the Linji school's later prestige. It is a basic text of Rinzai Zen and was one of the first Zen works translated into Western languages.
image_caption: Linji Yixuan, Japanese ink portrait

title: Blue Cliff Record (Biyan lu)
creator: yuanwu-keqin
note: One hundred kōans with verses by Xuedou and commentary by Yuanwu Keqin, the most celebrated work of kōan literature.
description: Each case gives an introduction, a classic exchange between Chan masters, such as Emperor Wu questioning Bodhidharma or Zhaozhou's 'Wash your bowl', with Xuedou Chongxian's verse, and Yuanwu's comments and interlinear notes, often ironic and allusive. Yuanwu's lectures at the Blue Cliff Hall at Jiashan were compiled by his students in 1125. Tradition says his disciple Dahui burned the blocks because students were memorising it instead of practising; it was reprinted in 1300. In Japan, as the Hekiganroku, it became central to Rinzai training.

title: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan)
creator: wumen-huikai
note: Forty-eight kōans with Wumen's comments and verses, opening with Zhaozhou's 'Mu'; the most used kōan collection in Zen training.
description: Wumen Huikai compiled the collection for his students in 1228, choosing short cases such as Zhaozhou's dog, Gutei's finger, Nanquan killing the cat and the Buddha holding up a flower, and adding a pithy comment and a four-line verse to each. His comment on the first case urges students to concentrate on 'Mu' with their whole body until doubt and understanding break open, a method linked to Dahui's 'phrase-contemplation'. Brought to Japan in 1254 by Shinchi Kakushin, the Mumonkan became a standard text of Rinzai Zen and, through twentieth-century translations, of Western Zen.
image_caption: Page of a Japanese edition of the Mumonkan

title: Ten Oxherding Pictures (Shiniu tu)
creator: kuoan-shiyuan
location: Song China; best-known version painted by Tenshō Shūbun in 15th-century Japan (Shōkoku-ji, Kyoto)
note: Ten pictures and verses showing the search for, taming and forgetting of an ox, the classic image of the stages of Zen practice.
description: Kuoan's sequence begins with a herdsman searching for a lost ox, the true mind, finding its tracks, glimpsing it, catching, taming and riding it home; then the ox is forgotten, both ox and self are forgotten in an empty circle, there is a return to the source, and finally the sage enters the marketplace 'with helping hands'. Its ending, where awakening returns to ordinary compassion, distinguishes it from earlier sequences that ended in emptiness. Painted by Shūbun and many others in Japan and still used in teaching, it is one of the most widely reproduced images of Zen.
image_caption: Tenshō Shūbun (attributed), Searching for the Ox, from the Ten Oxherding Pictures, 15th century

title: Library Cave of Dunhuang (Mogao Cave 17)
creator: dunhuang-monks
location: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang; contents now in London, Paris, Beijing, St Petersburg, Kyoto and elsewhere
note: A small chamber packed with some 50,000 manuscripts, prints and paintings of the fifth to eleventh centuries, the greatest single source for medieval Chinese religion.
description: Cave 17 opens off the corridor of Cave 16 and was first a memorial chapel to the monk Hongbian, whose portrait statue stood in it. Around 1000, for reasons still debated, perhaps to store sacred waste or out of fear of invasion, it was filled with documents and sealed. The Daoist Wang Yuanlu found it in 1900. Aurel Stein in 1907 and Paul Pelliot in 1908 bought thousands of items, and others went to Japan, Russia and Beijing. The cache contains Buddhist sutras in many languages, the earliest Chan texts and the Platform Sutra, Daoist and Manichaean scriptures, Christian texts of the Church of the East, popular ballads, contracts and letters, and the printed Diamond Sutra of 868. International digitisation projects have begun to reunite it.
image_file: Photo showing Cave 16 and the manuscripts piled up for Stein to examine near the entrance to Cave 17, the “library cave.jpg
image_caption: Manuscripts from the Library Cave piled for Aurel Stein near its entrance, 1907

title: Humanistic Buddhism and the journal Haichao yin
creator: taixu
note: The 'Sound of the Tide', the journal Taixu founded in 1920 to promote his reform of Chinese Buddhism for life in this world.
description: Haichao yin, founded by Taixu and his disciples in 1920, became the longest-running Chinese Buddhist periodical, carrying debates on monastic education, property, Buddhism and science, and Buddhist responses to Christianity and Marxism. In its pages and in lectures such as those on 'Buddhism of human life' (rensheng fojiao), Taixu argued that Buddhism should centre on human beings and social service rather than rites for the dead. His approach, developed by Yinshun, became Humanistic Buddhism, the dominant ideal of modern Chinese Buddhism in Taiwan and beyond.

title: Taima Mandala
creator: nara-buddhist-workshops
type: Woven mandala of the Pure Land
location: Taima-dera, Nara Prefecture; copies in many collections
note: A great silk tapestry of Amitābha's Pure Land after the Contemplation Sutra, believed by legend to have been woven from lotus threads by Princess Chūjō.
description: The original Taima Mandala, about four metres square and now badly damaged, is a tapestry probably woven in Tang China or by immigrant weavers in Japan in the eighth century. Its centre shows Amitābha's paradise with palaces, ponds and bodhisattvas; its borders depict Queen Vaidehī's story and the sixteen contemplations, following Shandao's reading of the sutra. In the medieval legend of Chūjōhime, a princess wove it with the help of Amida in a single night in 763. From the thirteenth century Pure Land preachers, especially of the Seizan branch, circulated painted copies and used them in sermons, so it became one of the most reproduced images of Japanese Buddhism.
image_file: Taima Mandala, 14th century, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 57.156.6.jpg
image_caption: Painted copy of the Taima Mandala, 14th century (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

title: Hyakumantō Darani (One Million Pagoda Charms)
creator: empress-shotoku
type: Printed dhāraṇī charms in miniature pagodas
location: Ten great temples of Nara; about 40,000 pagodas survive at Hōryū-ji
note: A million tiny wooden pagodas, each holding a printed Buddhist spell, made at the order of Empress Shōtoku: among the world's oldest surviving printed texts.
description: After the defeat of Fujiwara no Nakamaro's rebellion in 764, Empress Shōtoku vowed to make a million pagodas; according to the Shoku Nihongi they were completed in 770. Each three-storey pagoda, turned on a lathe and about 21 centimetres high, contains a small paper roll printed with one of four dhāraṇī from the Sutra of the Great Dhāraṇī of Stainless Pure Light, a text promising long life and the removal of sins. Whether they were printed from wood or metal plates is debated. The pagodas were distributed to ten temples; Hōryū-ji kept many thousands, some of which were sold in the Meiji period and are now in museums worldwide. They show the protective, ritual purpose of early Buddhist printing.
image_caption: A Hyakumantō pagoda and its printed dhāraṇī

title: Miraculous Tales of Japan (Nihon ryōiki)
creator: kyokai
location: Nara; oldest manuscripts at Kōfuku-ji and Raigō-in
note: Kyōkai's 116 stories of karmic reward and punishment in Japan, the first collection of Japanese Buddhist tales.
description: The full title, Nihonkoku genpō zen'aku ryōiki, means 'records of miraculous karmic retribution of good and evil in Japan'. Written in Chinese with Japanese elements, the tales, arranged chronologically from the fifth to the early ninth century, tell of people reborn as oxen for unpaid debts, hunters punished, images that bleed or speak, women saved by devotion to Kannon, the ascetic En no Gyōja flying over mountains, and the monk Gyōki teaching the people. Kyōkai aimed to prove that karma operates in Japan as in China and India. The collection shaped later setsuwa literature such as the Konjaku monogatarishū and is a basic source for early Japanese popular religion.
image_caption: Kōfuku-ji manuscript of the Nihon ryōiki

title: Regulations for Students of the Mountain School (Sange gakushō shiki)
creator: saicho
location: Mount Hiei; Saichō's autograph in the Tendai hokkeshū nenbun engi (Enryaku-ji)
note: Saichō's petitions to the court for a Mahāyāna ordination platform on Mount Hiei and a twelve-year training of 'treasures of the nation'.
description: The three documents, in six, eight and four articles, were submitted to Emperor Saga in 818 and 819. Saichō asked that Tendai's annual ordinands receive only the bodhisattva precepts of the Brahmā's Net Sutra on Mount Hiei, rather than the full monastic precepts at the Nara-controlled platform of Tōdai-ji, and that they then remain on the mountain for twelve years of study and practice. He called those who could speak and act on the Way 'treasures of the nation'. The Nara clergy objected; Saichō answered in his Kenkairon, and permission came only after his death in 822. The independent Hiei ordination made Enryaku-ji the main training centre of Japanese Buddhism.
image_caption: Tendai hokkeshū nenbun engi, Saichō's petitions in his own hand (Enryaku-ji)

title: Catalogue of Imported Items (Go-shōrai mokuroku)
creator: kukai
location: Dazaifu; copy attributed to Saichō at Tō-ji, Kyoto
note: Kūkai's report to the throne listing the scriptures, mandalas, ritual implements and relics he brought back from China, and announcing the esoteric teaching.
description: Writing from Dazaifu in Kyushu after returning early from China, Kūkai listed 216 works in 461 fascicles, many newly translated by Amoghavajra, as well as mandalas and portraits of patriarchs, ritual implements and relics, all received from his master Huiguo. He explained that the esoteric teaching was the swiftest path to buddhahood and described his initiation. The catalogue was meant to justify his early return and win court support, which it did after a delay. A copy traditionally attributed to Saichō, who borrowed texts from Kūkai, is a National Treasure at Tō-ji.
image_caption: Kūkai's Catalogue of Imported Items, Tō-ji copy

title: Mandalas of the Two Realms (Ryōkai mandara)
creator: kukai
note: The paired Womb Realm and Diamond Realm mandalas of Shingon, maps of the cosmic Buddha Mahāvairocana and the deities emanating from him.
description: The Womb Realm (Taizōkai) mandala, based on the Mahāvairocana Sutra, shows Mahāvairocana at the centre of an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by concentric courts of buddhas, bodhisattvas and guardians, expressing the principle of compassion; the Diamond Realm (Kongōkai), based on the Vajraśekhara texts, arranges nine assemblies in a grid expressing wisdom. Kūkai brought a pair painted in Chang'an under Huiguo's direction; the Takao Mandala at Jingo-ji, in gold and silver on purple silk, is the oldest surviving Japanese version. In Shingon ritual the mandalas are used for initiation, where the initiate throws a flower onto the mandala to find a personal deity, and for meditation.
image_caption: The Womb Realm (Taizōkai) mandala, Tō-ji, Kyoto

title: Attaining Enlightenment in This Very Body (Sokushin jōbutsu gi)
creator: kukai
note: Kūkai's short treatise on how Shingon ritual allows buddhahood in this life; its philosophy is treated in the philosophy section.
description: Kūkai's treatise interprets a two-stanza verse to show that the six elements, earth, water, fire, wind, space and consciousness, that make up all things are the body of Mahāvairocana, that the four kinds of mandala express it, and that through the 'three mysteries', mudrā, mantra and meditative union, the practitioner's body, speech and mind become one with the Buddha's. For the history of religion it is the charter of Shingon practice and of the wider Japanese idea that buddhahood is immediate. The cult of Kūkai as one who entered eternal meditation in his body at Kōya made this doctrine visible to pilgrims.

title: Essentials of Rebirth in the Pure Land (Ōjōyōshū)
creator: genshin
note: Genshin's anthology on the horrors of the six realms and the bliss of Amida's land, with instructions for nenbutsu and deathbed rites.
description: In ten chapters drawn from some 160 scriptures and treatises, Genshin first describes with terrible vividness the eight great hells and the other realms of rebirth, so that the reader will 'loathe this defiled world', then the joys of the Pure Land, and finally methods of practice, above all contemplating Amida's form and calling his name, and the conduct of the deathbed, where the dying hold a cord tied to an image of Amida. It became the guide for Heian aristocrats such as Fujiwara no Michinaga, inspired hell scrolls and paintings of Amida's descent, and was sent to Song China, where it was admired. Hōnen's turn to exclusive nenbutsu began from it.

title: Passages on the Nenbutsu Selected in the Primal Vow (Senchaku hongan nenbutsu shū)
creator: honen
location: Kyoto, written for the regent Kujō Kanezane
note: Hōnen's argument that Amida chose recitation of his name as the one practice for salvation, the founding text of the Jōdo school.
description: Written at the request of the former regent Kujō Kanezane, the Senchakushū in sixteen chapters quotes scriptures and Shandao's commentary, adding Hōnen's own explanations. It divides Buddhism into the difficult Path of Sages and the easy Pure Land path, and argues that Amida, in his eighteenth vow, selected the nenbutsu above all other practices because it is easy for everyone, so that other practices should be set aside. Hōnen allowed only close disciples to copy it during his life. After its publication it was attacked by the monk Myōe for denying the aspiration to enlightenment, and in 1227 Enryaku-ji monks burned its printing blocks. It is the basic text of Jōdo-shū.

title: One-Sheet Document (Ichimai kishōmon)
creator: honen
note: Hōnen's last testament, a single sheet stating that nothing is needed but to say the nenbutsu with the conviction of rebirth.
description: Two days before his death in 1212, at a disciple's request, Hōnen wrote a short statement summarising his teaching: the nenbutsu he taught was not the contemplative practice of Chinese and Japanese scholars nor a fruit of learning, but simply saying 'Namu Amida Butsu' in the belief that one will be reborn; even those who have studied all the Buddha's teaching should become like the ignorant and simply recite. It is recited daily in Jōdo temples and is regarded as the essence of his teaching.

title: Teaching, Practice, Faith and Realisation (Kyōgyōshinshō)
creator: shinran
location: Inada, Hitachi Province, and Kyoto; autograph Bandō manuscript at Higashi Hongan-ji
note: Shinran's systematic anthology of scriptural passages with commentary, the foundational text of Jōdo Shinshū; its philosophy is treated in the philosophy section.
description: In six books on the true teaching (the Sutra of Infinite Life), practice (the name), faith (shinjin), realisation, the true Buddha and land, and the provisional and false, Shinran assembles quotations from sutras and the seven Pure Land patriarchs of India, China and Japan, interpreting them so that every element of salvation becomes the work of Amida's 'other power'. He wrote and revised it over decades; the date 1224 often taken as Jōdo Shinshū's founding comes from a passage within it. The hymn 'Shōshinge' from its second book is chanted daily by Shin Buddhists. Shinran's autograph copy survives.
image_caption: Shinran's autograph manuscript of the Kyōgyōshinshō (Bandō edition)

title: Treatise on Promoting Zen for the Protection of the Country (Kōzen gokokuron)
creator: eisai
note: Eisai's defence of Zen against the Tendai establishment, arguing that strict Zen discipline would protect the state.
description: Faced with a court ban on the 'Daruma school' in 1194, Eisai wrote this treatise in ten sections to show that the Zen he had received in China was orthodox, that Saichō himself had transmitted Chan along with Tendai, and that Zen practice depends on keeping the precepts. He argued that if monks observe discipline and meditate the nation will be secure, aligning Zen with the 'state-protecting' role of established Buddhism. The text helped secure shogunal patronage and the foundation of Kennin-ji, and marks the start of Rinzai Zen as an institution in Japan.

title: Drinking Tea for Health (Kissa yōjōki)
creator: eisai
location: Kamakura; presented to the shōgun Minamoto no Sanetomo
note: Eisai's treatise on the medicinal virtues of tea and mulberry, the first Japanese book on tea.
description: Eisai explains, with references to Chinese medicine and five-phases theory, that tea strengthens the heart, the organ most in need in Japan, and describes how tea was grown and prepared in Song China. According to the Azuma kagami, he presented the revised version in 1214 to the shōgun Minamoto no Sanetomo, who was suffering after a night of drinking. The text connected the monastic tea culture of Chan with Japanese elite life and is honoured as a founding document of the Japanese way of tea.
image_file: 喫茶養生記-Kissa Yōjōki, Vol.1, p.4.png
image_caption: Page from an early edition of the Kissa yōjōki

title: Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō)
creator: dogen
location: Kōshō-ji near Kyoto and Eihei-ji, Echizen
note: Dōgen's collection of essays in Japanese on practice, time, being and monastic life, the central text of Sōtō Zen; its philosophy is treated in the philosophy section.
description: Dōgen wrote the 75 and 12 fascicles of the Shōbōgenzō over two decades, in a dense, inventive Japanese full of quotations of Chinese kōans. Beside essays such as 'Being-Time' and 'Genjō kōan', many fascicles prescribe practice: how to sit, how to wash the face, how to wear the robe, how to receive the precepts, on the merits of leaving home. For the religious history of Sōtō it was long a treasure guarded by the monasteries and hardly read; the 95-fascicle printed edition of 1796–1815 and twentieth-century philosophers made it famous. The Shushōgi, an anthology from it compiled in 1890, became the standard Sōtō lay liturgy.

title: Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo kyōkun)
creator: dogen
note: Dōgen's instructions for the monastery cook, treating the preparation of meals as Zen practice.
description: Dōgen recalls how, on arriving in China in 1223, he met an old monastery cook who had walked miles to buy mushrooms and told him that cooking was his practice, and another drying seaweed in the midday sun who would not leave the task to others. He then sets out the cook's duties: planning meals with the officers, washing rice, handling each ingredient with care, and cultivating 'joyful mind, nurturing mind and great mind'. Later included in the Eihei shingi, Dōgen's monastic code, it remains a guide for Zen kitchens and a popular text in the modern world.

title: Establishing the Correct Teaching for the Peace of the Land (Risshō ankoku ron)
creator: nichiren
note: Nichiren's warning to the Kamakura regent that disasters would continue, and foreign invasion come, unless the state abandoned Hōnen's Pure Land teaching.
description: Written after a series of earthquakes, famines and epidemics, the treatise is a dialogue between a host and a traveller. The host argues, from the Lotus, Golden Light and other sutras, that the protective gods have abandoned Japan because people follow the false teaching of Hōnen's Senchakushū, and predicts internal rebellion and foreign invasion if this continues. Nichiren presented it to the retired regent Hōjō Tokiyori in 1260; the result was an attack on his hut and exile to Izu. The Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 seemed to his followers to fulfil the prophecy. It remains the central statement of Nichiren's vision of religion and nation.
image_caption: Manuscript of the Risshō ankoku ron

title: Opening of the Eyes (Kaimokushō)
creator: nichiren
note: Nichiren's treatise from exile on Sado, identifying himself as the votary of the Lotus Sutra whose sufferings fulfil its prophecies.
description: After the near-execution at Tatsunokuchi in 1271 and banishment to the island of Sado, Nichiren wrote this long work in a freezing hut. It surveys the teachings of Confucianism, Brahmanism and the Buddhist schools to show the supremacy of the Lotus Sutra, asks why, if he truly upholds it, he is not protected by the gods, and answers that his persecutions are exactly what the sutra predicts for its practitioners in the latter age. It ends with his vow to be 'the pillar, the eyes and the great ship of Japan'. With the Kanjin no honzonshō, it is one of his most important writings.

title: Gohonzon mandala of Nichiren
creator: nichiren
location: Various Nichiren temples, such as Myōhon-ji and Taiseki-ji
note: The calligraphic mandalas Nichiren inscribed as objects of worship, with the title of the Lotus Sutra in the centre surrounded by the names of buddhas and gods.
description: From 1271 Nichiren wrote on paper or silk a vertical inscription of the daimoku, Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō, flanked by the names of Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna, bodhisattvas, Indian and Chinese teachers, Buddhist protectors and the Japanese kami Amaterasu and Hachiman, depicting the assembly of the Lotus Sutra. Some 120 survive in his hand. Chanting the daimoku before a gohonzon is the central practice of Nichiren Buddhism. Which mandala is authoritative is a major point of difference between Nichiren schools, with Nichiren Shōshū venerating the Dai-Gohonzon of Taiseki-ji, whose authenticity other schools dispute.
image_caption: A gohonzon mandala attributed to Nichiren

title: Letters (Ofumi)
creator: rennyo
note: Rennyo's simple letters explaining Shinran's teaching of faith, read aloud at gatherings, which made Jōdo Shinshū a mass religion.
description: Rennyo wrote hundreds of short letters to followers and congregations in plain Japanese mixed script, explaining that one is saved at the moment of entrusting oneself to Amida, that the nenbutsu is an expression of gratitude, and that believers should respect gods, buddhas and secular authorities while holding faith in their hearts. His grandson Ennyo selected 80 into five fascicles, the Gojō ofumi (called Gobunshō in the Ōtani branch), which are read at Shin Buddhist services. The 'Letter on White Ashes', on the impermanence of life, is recited at funerals.

title: Crazy Cloud Anthology (Kyōunshū)
creator: ikkyu
note: Ikkyū's collection of about a thousand Chinese verses, mixing Zen insight, satire of monastic hypocrisy and frank love poems.
description: Ikkyū called himself Kyōun, 'Crazy Cloud'. The poems, collected by disciples, range from verses on kōans and Zen masters to attacks on his rival Yōsō of Daitoku-ji for selling enlightenment, celebrations of sake and the brothel, and late love poems to the blind singer Mori, whom he met in his seventies. They express the idea that awakening is found in, not beyond, the passions, and the defiance of convention associated with Zen 'madness'. The collection survives in several manuscripts, with a sequel, and has been widely translated.

title: Song of Zazen and Orategama
creator: hakuin
note: Hakuin's popular hymn on seated meditation and his letters on Zen practice in daily life, written in Japanese for lay people.
description: The Zazen wasan, a hymn of some 44 lines in Japanese, begins by declaring that all beings are originally buddhas, like water and ice, and praises zazen as the gate to awakening; it is chanted in Rinzai temples to this day. The Orategama, 'Embossed Tea Kettle', printed in 1751, collects letters to a feudal lord, a nun and a sick monk explaining how to practise kōan meditation amid daily affairs and describing methods of healing exhausted body and mind. Like his other vernacular works and songs, they show how Hakuin carried Zen beyond the monastery.

title: Daruma paintings
creator: hakuin
location: Many collections, e.g. Metropolitan Museum of Art, Eisei Bunko, Manju-ji (Ōita)
note: Hakuin's bold ink portraits of Bodhidharma, painted by the hundreds as teaching tools and gifts.
description: Hakuin took up painting and calligraphy seriously in his sixties and produced thousands of works, which he gave to visitors and lay followers. His Daruma figures, with glaring eyes and thick robes drawn in a few heavy strokes, are often inscribed with phrases such as 'Point directly at the human mind; see your nature and become Buddha'. Unconcerned with professional polish, they belong to the tradition of zenga, Zen paintings by monks. Rediscovered by collectors in the twentieth century, they are now among the best-known images of Zen.
image_file: Hakuin Ekaku - Portrait of Daruma - 2015.500.9.3 - Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg
image_caption: Hakuin Ekaku, Daruma, ink on paper (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

title: Chronicles of Japan (Nihon Shoki)
creator: prince-toneri
location: Nara; earliest fragments 9th century, Tanaka manuscript (Nara National Museum)
note: Japan's first official history in thirty books, opening with the age of the gods: with the Kojiki the basic source of Shinto mythology.
description: Presented to the throne in 720 by Prince Toneri, the Nihon Shoki was written in classical Chinese on the model of Chinese dynastic histories. Its first two books tell of the creation of the islands by Izanagi and Izanami, the sun goddess Amaterasu and her brother Susanoo, and the descent of her grandson to rule Japan, giving many variant versions ('in one writing it says…'); the rest narrate reigns from the legendary first emperor Jimmu to Empress Jitō in 697, including the official introduction of Buddhism from Baekje in 552. The parallel Kojiki of 712, a literary classic, is treated in the literature section. The Nihon Shoki was lectured on at court from 721, was the object of medieval Shinto commentaries, and was used in the Meiji period to support emperor worship; historians treat its early chronology as legendary.
image_caption: Fragment of the Tanaka manuscript of the Nihon Shoki, 9th century

title: Procedures of the Engi Era (Engishiki), books on the kami
creator: engishiki-compilers
type: Code of procedures with ritual prayers
location: Heian-kyō (Kyoto); oldest manuscripts include the Kujō family copy (Tokyo National Museum)
note: The Heian code whose first ten books register the official shrines of Japan and preserve the oldest Shinto ritual prayers (norito).
description: The Engishiki in fifty books regulated the whole of court administration. Books one to ten, on kami affairs, set out the festivals of the year, such as the Kinensai prayer for harvest, the Niiname harvest offering and the great Daijōsai at an accession, the offerings each shrine was to receive, the rites of the Ise priestess and of purification, and a register (jinmyōchō) of 3,132 deities in 2,861 shrines. Book eight records 27 norito, including the Great Purification (Ōharae) recited twice a year to remove the sins of the nation, which is still in use. The Engishiki is the fundamental source for early shrine religion and its listing gives shrines prestige to this day.
image_file: Engishiki Jingi cropped Engishiki Vol 2 Flame 37.jpg
image_caption: Page from the books on the kami (Jingi) of an early Engishiki manuscript

title: Illustrated Legends of Kitano Tenjin (Kitano Tenjin engi emaki)
creator: yamato-e-painters
note: Handscrolls telling how the exiled minister Sugawara no Michizane became the angry god Tenjin and was enshrined at Kitano, with vivid scenes of the Buddhist hells.
description: Sugawara no Michizane (845–903), a scholar and minister exiled to Dazaifu through the intrigues of the Fujiwara, died in disgrace; when lightning, plague and deaths struck the court, they were attributed to his angry spirit, and he was enshrined at Kitano in Kyoto in 947 as Tenjin, later a god of learning. The Jōkyū version of the scrolls, dated around 1219 and painted in yamato-e, narrates his life, exile and the vengeance of his spirit, and then the visions of the monk Nichizō, who travels through the six realms and the hells. It shows how kami cults, angry-spirit (goryō) beliefs and Buddhist cosmology fused in medieval Japan, and served as the shrine's origin legend.
image_file: Kitano Tenjin Engi Emaki - Jokyo - Michizane in exil.jpg
image_caption: Michizane in exile, from the Jōkyū version of the Kitano Tenjin engi emaki

title: Five Books of Shinto (Shintō gobusho)
creator: ise-priesthood
note: Texts produced by the Watarai priests of Ise's Outer Shrine, the founding works of Ise Shinto, presented as ancient records.
description: The five texts claim to be records from the time of the shrine's founding but were written, scholars agree, by Watarai priests in the thirteenth century; Watarai Yukitada is often named. They elevate Toyouke, the deity of the Outer Shrine, to equality with Amaterasu by identifying her with the primordial kami Ame-no-minakanushi, and they teach that purity and honesty (shōjiki) are the essence of kami worship. Drawing on Buddhist esoteric and Chinese cosmological ideas while asserting the priority of the kami, they shaped Watarai Ieyuki's systematic Ise Shinto, Yoshida Kanetomo and Edo-period Confucian Shinto. Exposed as forgeries by Edo scholars, they remain important as the first Shinto theology.
image_caption: The Outer Shrine (Gekū) at Ise, seat of the Watarai priests

title: Periodic rebuilding of the Ise Shrines (Shikinen Sengū)
creator: ise-priesthood
note: The rite of rebuilding the shrines of Ise on an adjacent site about every twenty years and transferring the deity at night.
description: According to shrine records, the first periodic rebuilding of the Inner Shrine took place in 690 under Empress Jitō. Every twenty years, in principle, new main halls and some 65 other buildings are built of cypress on the alternate site beside the old, with all the treasures and costumes remade, and in the culminating ceremony (sengyo) the sacred mirror of Amaterasu is carried at night in procession to the new hall. The cycle was interrupted for over a century in the age of civil war and restored in 1585. The rite renews purity and transmits building and craft skills; the architecture of the shrines is a subject for the architecture section.
image_file: Ise Daijingu sengyo no zu 伊勢太神宮遷御之図 (Depiction of the Relocation of the Grand Shrine of Ise) (BM 2008,3037.21409).jpg
image_caption: Woodblock print of the night transfer (sengyo) of the deity at Ise (British Museum)

title: Essentials of Yuiitsu Shinto (Yuiitsu Shintō myōbō yōshū)
creator: yoshida-kanetomo
note: Yoshida Kanetomo's exposition of 'one and only' Shinto, which he claimed as the root of which Buddhism and Confucianism are the flowers and branches.
description: Framed as a dialogue and attributed by Kanetomo to his remote ancestor Urabe Kanenobu, the treatise distinguishes three kinds of Shinto: that combined with Buddhism, that based on shrine origin legends, and the 'primordial' Yuiitsu Shinto transmitted secretly in the Urabe-Yoshida line. It describes esoteric rites modelled on Shingon ones and quotes a saying attributed to Prince Shōtoku that Shinto is the root, Confucianism the branches and Buddhism the fruit. Though based on invented authorities, it gave Shinto an independent doctrine and liturgy, and the Yoshida house used it to dominate shrine priesthood until the Meiji Restoration.

title: The True Pillar of the Soul (Tama no mihashira)
creator: hirata-atsutane
type: Shinto cosmology and theology of the afterlife
note: Hirata Atsutane's account of the creation of the cosmos and the fate of the soul, which gave Restoration Shinto a doctrine of the afterlife.
description: Using diagrams in the manner of Hattori Nakatsune's Sandaikō, Hirata describes the formation of heaven, earth and the underworld from the creative kami and argues that the dead do not go to the polluted land of Yomi, as Motoori Norinaga held, but remain in an unseen realm (yūmei) within this world, ruled by Ōkuninushi, close to their descendants. He presents this knowledge as the foundation of a steadfast Japanese spirit. The work was widely read among his disciples, helped shape Shinto funerals and ancestor rites, and influenced the religious policy of the early Meiji government.
image_caption: Diagram from the Tama no mihashira

title: Arouse Your Mind and Practise (Balsim suhaeng jang)
creator: wonhyo
note: Wonhyo's short exhortation to leave worldly attachments and practise, read by every novice in Korean monasteries.
description: In rhythmic Chinese prose, Wonhyo contrasts the buddhas, who abandoned desires and practised austerities in the mountains, with ordinary people who cling to wealth and pleasure, reminds the reader that life is short and death certain, and urges immediate practice and precepts. Attributed to Wonhyo by tradition, it was combined with texts by Jinul and Yaun into the Chobalsim jagyeongmun, the primer that Korean novices memorise to this day, so that it is among the most widely read Korean Buddhist texts.

title: Vow at the White Lotus Site (Baekhwa doryang barwonmun)
creator: uisang
note: A short vow attributed to Uisang, expressing devotion to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara at his sacred cave on the east coast.
description: According to the Samguk yusa, Uisang prayed at a sea cave at Naksan until Avalokiteśvara appeared and instructed him to build a temple, which became Naksansa. This vow, attributed to him, describes the practitioner's wish to become one with the bodhisattva, to be born in the White Lotus land and to save beings as the bodhisattva does. It is an early example of the cult of Avalokiteśvara that made Naksansa and its hermitage Hongnyeonam one of Korea's principal pilgrimage sites.

title: New Catalogue of the Teachings of All Schools (Sinpyeon jejong gyojang chongnok)
creator: uicheon
note: Uicheon's catalogue of some 1,010 East Asian Buddhist commentaries, compiled to collect and print the scholarship missing from the canon.
description: The Buddhist canon included sutras, monastic rules and Indian treatises but not most Chinese, Korean and Khitan commentaries. Uicheon, having gathered such works in Song China, Liao and Japan, catalogued about 1,010 titles in 4,857 fascicles by scripture and had many of them carved as a 'supplementary canon' (gyojang) at Heungwangsa. Most of the blocks were lost in the Mongol invasions, but some prints survive in Japan, and the catalogue preserves the titles of works otherwise unknown. It is a landmark of East Asian Buddhist bibliography.

title: Tripitaka Koreana (Palman daejanggyeong)
creator: tripitaka-koreana-carvers
note: The complete Buddhist canon carved on 81,258 woodblocks during the Mongol invasions, the oldest intact and most accurate woodblock canon.
description: Begun to win the Buddha's protection against the Mongols after the first Goryeo canon was burned in 1232, the canon comprises 1,516 titles in some 6,800 fascicles. The blocks, of birch and other woods seasoned in seawater and coated with lacquer, carry 23 lines of 14 characters per side and are reinforced at the ends with metal. The editor Sugi collated earlier Chinese and Korean editions and recorded his corrections in a separate work. Since 1398 the blocks have been stored at Haeinsa in the Janggyeong panjeon halls, designed with slatted windows and charcoal-laced floors to control humidity. Prints from them were sought by Japanese rulers in the Joseon era, and they underlie the modern Taishō canon. Both the blocks and the halls are UNESCO heritage.
image_caption: Woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana at Haeinsa

title: Compact of the Samādhi and Prajñā Society (Jeonghye gyeolsa mun)
creator: jinul
note: Jinul's call to monks to form a retreat community practising meditation and wisdom together, the founding document of the Songgwangsa tradition.
description: Jinul recalls the vow he and his fellow monks made in 1182 to leave the corrupt capital monasteries, and argues that in the age of the decline of the Dharma one should still practise concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) together, since the mind is fundamentally the Buddha. He answers objections from Pure Land devotees and doctrinal scholars, insisting that his community welcomes practitioners of all schools. The society moved in 1200 to the temple Jinul renamed Suseonsa, today's Songgwangsa, and became the model of Korean Seon practice.

title: Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms (Samguk yusa)
creator: iryeon
type: Collection of history, myth and Buddhist legend
note: Iryeon's collection of Korean foundation myths, Buddhist miracle stories and hyangga songs, including the Dangun myth.
description: In five books, Iryeon gathered material ignored by the Confucian History of the Three Kingdoms: the founding myth of Gojoseon by Dangun, son of the Heavenly Prince and a bear-woman, the birth legends of Silla, Goguryeo and Gaya kings, and above all Buddhist history: the arrival of Buddhism in each kingdom, the martyrdom of Ichadon, temple origins, images and relics, eminent monks such as Wonhyo and Uisang, and miracles of devotion. His sources included lost histories, inscriptions and oral tales. It preserves fourteen of the 25 surviving hyangga, and its Dangun story became central to modern Korean national identity.
image_file: Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms in museum.jpg
image_caption: Early printed edition of the Samguk yusa on display

title: Jikji (Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol)
creator: baegun
type: Seon anthology printed with movable metal type
location: Printed at Heungdeoksa, Cheongju; volume 2 in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris
note: An anthology of the teachings of buddhas and Seon patriarchs, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
description: Baegun selected passages from Chan transmission records on recognising the true mind, beginning with the seven buddhas of the past and continuing through Indian and Chinese patriarchs. His disciples Seokchan and Daldam printed it in two volumes in the seventh month of 1377 at Heungdeoksa, a temple outside Cheongju, as the colophon states. Only the second volume survives, lacking its first leaf; it was acquired by the French diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy in Seoul and passed through the collector Henri Vever to the Bibliothèque nationale in 1950. Its rediscovery in 1972 established Korean priority in metal-type printing, and it is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World. Korea has long sought its return.
image_file: Korean book-Jikji-Selected Teachings of Buddhist Sages and Seon Masters-1377.jpg
image_caption: A page of the Jikji, printed with metal type in 1377

title: Mirror for Seon Students (Seonga gwigam)
creator: seosan
note: Seosan's concise manual of Seon practice, combining meditation with scripture and recitation, the standard guide of Joseon Buddhism.
description: Seosan gathered essential passages from sutras and Chan records, each with his comment, to guide students in an era when Buddhism was restricted by the Confucian state. He teaches that the scriptures are the Buddha's words and Seon his mind, so that one should study the teachings and then set them aside to investigate a huatou, and he includes guidance on Pure Land recitation and monastic conduct. Written in Chinese and translated into Korean, it was reprinted in Japan, and remains a basic text of the Jogye Order.

title: Great Buddhist Scripture (Bulgyo daejeon)
creator: han-yong-un
note: Han Yong-un's one-volume anthology of passages from the Buddhist canon, arranged by theme for modern readers.
description: While studying the Tripitaka Koreana at Tongdosa, Han Yong-un selected passages from over 400 scriptures and treatises and arranged them in nine chapters on such topics as faith, the self, society, the nation and practice, so that lay people could grasp Buddhism without the full canon. Published in 1914, it embodied his reformist conviction, set out in his treatise on Korean Buddhist reform, that Buddhism should be accessible, socially engaged and modern. It was one of the first works of its kind in East Asia.

title: Princess Bari (Barigongju)
creator: korean-shamans
location: Sung in rituals for the dead across Korea
note: The shaman myth of the abandoned seventh princess who journeys to the underworld for healing water and becomes the guide of the dead.
description: Sung in the rituals that send the dead to the other world, such as the Seoul saenamgut, the narrative tells of a king who abandons his seventh daughter because he wanted a son. When he falls mortally ill, his other daughters refuse to help, but Bari, raised by an old couple, travels to the realm of the dead, serves a guardian for years, marries him and bears sons, and brings back the water of life that revives her father. Refusing worldly reward, she becomes the deity who guides souls and the ancestress of shamans. Recorded in over a hundred versions, it is a major work of Korean oral literature and has inspired modern novels and plays.
image_file: Spirit of a Noble Woman (Probably Princess Pari) and Attendant LACMA M.2000.15.11.jpg
image_caption: Shaman painting of a noble woman, probably Princess Bari, with attendant (Los Angeles County Museum of Art)

title: Shamanic deity paintings (musindo)
creator: korean-shamans
location: Shaman shrines; collections such as the Gahoe Museum, Seoul, and Musée Guimet, Paris
note: The paintings of gods hung in shamans' shrines and at rituals, from mountain gods and generals to the Seven Stars and Princess Bari.
description: A shaman's shrine (sindang) is hung with paintings of the deities she serves: the Mountain God with his tiger, the Heavenly King Jeseok, the Seven Stars of the Big Dipper, generals such as Choe Yeong, the Dragon King, the Smallpox spirit and the shaman's own ancestors. Painted by professional or amateur artists and sometimes by shamans, they are consecrated and believed to house the gods. Many were destroyed in campaigns against superstition or burned when a shaman died, so most surviving ones date from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The early nineteenth-century Mansindo, 'picture of ten thousand gods', shows the whole pantheon at once.
image_file: Mansindo (萬神圖), early 19th-c. Korean shamanic painting.jpg
image_caption: Mansindo, painting of the shamanic pantheon, early 19th century

title: Jeju Chilmeoridang Yeongdeunggut
creator: korean-shamans
year: traditional; 2nd month of the lunar calendar
note: The Jeju island rite welcoming and seeing off Yeongdeung, the goddess of wind, for the safety of divers and fishermen, listed by UNESCO in 2009.
description: Each year in the second lunar month the people of Jeju's fishing villages welcome the wind goddess Yeongdeung, who visits the island bringing seeds of seaweed and shellfish, and send her off two weeks later. At the Chilmeoridang shrine shamans conduct the welcoming rite, prayers for the sea and divination with millet, and launch a small straw boat to carry the goddess away. The rite is closely tied to the haenyeo, the island's women divers. Designated a national intangible heritage in 1980, it was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2009.
image_caption: Museum display of a Jeju shamanic ritual, Jeju Folklore and Natural History Museum

title: Xi'an Stele (Stele of the Propagation of the Luminous Religion of Daqin)
creator: jingjing
location: Chang'an; now in the Forest of Steles Museum, Xi'an
note: A stele of 781, composed by the priest Jingjing, recording 146 years of the Church of the East in Tang China in Chinese and Syriac.
description: The black limestone stele, nearly three metres tall, has a cross above a lotus and clouds at its head. Its Chinese text summarises Christian teaching on the Trinity, creation, the fall, the incarnation and baptism in vocabulary borrowed from Buddhism and Daoism, then recounts how the monk Aluoben arrived in 635, how Emperor Taizong approved the faith and how later emperors supported it; Syriac lists name the clergy. Buried perhaps after the anti-foreign persecutions of 845, it was unearthed around 1625, when Jesuits hailed it as proof of Christianity's ancient roots in China, and its authenticity, once questioned in Europe, is now accepted. It is the main monument of the first Christian presence in East Asia.
image_caption: Head of the Xi'an Stele with its cross and title, Forest of Steles Museum

title: Letters from Japan
creator: francis-xavier
location: Kagoshima, Yamaguchi and Cochin; printed in Europe from 1550s
note: Francis Xavier's letters to his Jesuit companions describing the people, religion and prospects of Japan, the first European accounts of Japanese culture.
description: In his long letter from Kagoshima of November 1549 Xavier praised the Japanese as 'the best people yet discovered', curious, honourable and rational, described the Buddhist clergy and the questions he was asked about God, evil and the fate of unbaptised ancestors, and recommended sending learned missionaries who could debate. Later letters reported his journey to Kyoto, his change from poor clothing to formal dress to meet the lord of Yamaguchi, and his plan to go to China since the Japanese deferred to Chinese learning. Copied and printed in Europe, they launched the Jesuit mission, which by 1600 claimed some 300,000 Japanese Christians.

title: The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu shiyi)
creator: matteo-ricci
note: Ricci's dialogue between a Western and a Chinese scholar, presenting Christianity as the fulfilment of ancient Confucianism and refuting Buddhism and Daoism.
description: Written in classical Chinese after years of discussion with literati, the book argues by natural reason, quoting the Confucian classics, that there is one creator, the Lord of Heaven, identical with the Shangdi of the ancient texts; that the human soul is immortal and distinct from animals; and that Buddhist emptiness and Neo-Confucian principle cannot be the source of all things. It says little about Christ, leaving revelation for later instruction. It was widely read by scholars, included in the Siku quanshu catalogue of the Qing, and carried to Korea, where it inspired the first Catholic converts, and to Japan and Vietnam. Its method of accommodation was at the heart of the Chinese Rites controversy.

title: The Beginning of Heaven and Earth (Tenchi hajimari no koto)
creator: kakure-kirishitan
location: Sotome and Gotō Islands, Nagasaki region
note: The sacred narrative of the Hidden Christians, retelling the Bible from creation to Christ through Japanese folk tale and Buddhist ideas.
description: Transmitted orally and in manuscripts copied secretly, the text begins with the creation of the world by Deusu, tells of Adam and Eve and the flood, the birth of Christ to Maria, the massacre of the innocents, the crucifixion and the end of the world, in a form shaped by two centuries without priests: Maria is a princess of Luzon, the flood comes when the eyes of a temple lion turn red, and the dead are judged in Buddhist terms. Known from manuscripts copied in the nineteenth century and studied by twentieth-century folklorists, it is the main evidence for how the Kakure Kirishitan reinterpreted Christianity in isolation.

title: Maria Kannon images
creator: kakure-kirishitan
location: Nagasaki region; examples in the Tokyo National Museum and local collections
note: Statues of the Buddhist bodhisattva Kannon holding a child, venerated in secret by Hidden Christians as the Virgin Mary.
description: Under the ban on Christianity, believers around Nagasaki prayed before white porcelain figures of the child-giving Kannon, many made in Dehua in China, and other Buddhist images, which they understood as Maria with the infant Jesus, sometimes marking them with small crosses. Officials confiscated many in the persecutions of the 1850s and 1860s, and some passed to the Nagasaki magistrate's office and later to museums. The images show both the pressure of the Tokugawa inquisition and the creative fusion by which a forbidden faith survived.
image_caption: Maria Kannon figure, Edo period

title: Silk Letter (Hwang Sa-yeong baekseo)
creator: hwang-sa-yeong
location: Written in Jecheon, Joseon; now in the Vatican archives
note: A letter of some 13,000 characters on a piece of silk, describing the persecution of Korean Catholics and asking the bishop of Beijing for help.
description: Hiding during the Sinyu persecution of 1801, Hwang Sa-yeong wrote in minute characters on a silk cloth about 62 by 38 centimetres, intended to be carried to Bishop Alexandre de Gouveia in Beijing. He described the martyrdom of the priest Zhou Wenmo and many believers, the history of the Korean church founded by lay scholars, and proposed that the Pope ask the Qing emperor to protect Korean Christians, or even that Western ships and troops be sent to force toleration. Seized before it left Korea, it led to his execution and intensified persecution. Recovered from the Joseon archives in 1894 and given to the Pope in 1925, it is a key source for early Korean Catholicism and remains controversial for its appeal to foreign force.

title: Chinese Bible of Robert Morrison (Shentian shengshu)
creator: robert-morrison
note: The first complete Protestant translation of the Bible into Chinese, by Robert Morrison and William Milne.
description: Morrison translated the New Testament by 1813, drawing on a manuscript Catholic version found in the British Museum, and with William Milne the Old Testament, printing the complete Bible in 21 volumes at the Anglo-Chinese College in Malacca in 1823. Its style was stiff and later revised by Medhurst, Gützlaff and others, but it was the basis of the Protestant missionary Bible and of the tracts of Liang Fa, through which Hong Xiuquan learned of Christianity. The Taiping later printed a revised edition of a version descended from it.

title: Taiping Imperial Declarations (Taiping zhaoshu)
creator: hong-xiuquan
location: Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (printed in Yongan and Nanjing)
note: Hong Xiuquan's early religious tracts and edicts, setting out the Taiping faith in the Heavenly Father, the Heavenly Elder Brother Jesus and the destruction of 'demons'.
description: The Taiping zhaoshu gathers texts that Hong wrote in the 1840s, such as the 'Ode on the Original Way for Saving the World', in which he combines the worship of one God, called Shangdi as in Ricci's usage, with Confucian moral teaching and an account of an ancient China that had worshipped God before idolatry. Later Taiping publications, printed in Nanjing, included a revised Bible, the Ten Commandments and the account of Hong's vision of 1837. Most were destroyed after 1864 and survive chiefly in copies sent abroad by Western observers. They are the basic sources for the religious ideology of the largest civil war of the nineteenth century.

title: Ofudesaki (Tip of the Writing Brush)
creator: nakayama-miki
note: The 1,711 verses written by Nakayama Miki as God the Parent's revelation, the primary scripture of Tenrikyō.
description: In seventeen sections of waka-form verse written over thirteen years, Miki, writing as the brush of God the Parent, explains God's intention to save humanity and bring about the 'Joyous Life', the significance of the Jiba as the place of human creation, the Kanrodai pillar to be built there, the sweeping away of the mind's 'dust', and the coming salvation dance. Initially read only within the community, it was suppressed by the authorities in the period of State Shinto and officially published by Tenrikyō only in 1928. With the Mikagura-uta and Osashizu it forms the three scriptures of the religion.

title: Songs for the Service (Mikagura-uta)
creator: nakayama-miki
note: Nakayama Miki's songs, with dance and music, performed in the Tenrikyō service at the Jiba and in churches.
description: Beginning in 1866, Miki taught her followers songs composed in simple Japanese, numbering in all five sections, with hand movements and music played on traditional instruments. The central Kagura Service around the Kanrodai at the Jiba, performed by ten masked dancers, re-enacts the creation of humanity, while the Dance with Hand Movements is performed in all Tenrikyō churches. The songs speak of sweeping away the dust of the mind and building the joyous life. The authorities repeatedly arrested Miki and her followers for performing the service.

title: Great Scripture of Eastern Learning (Donggyeong daejeon)
creator: choe-je-u
location: Written in Gyeongju; printed by Choe Si-hyeong in Inje, Gangwon Province
note: Choe Je-u's writings in classical Chinese on his revelation and the teaching of Donghak, the scripture of Cheondogyo; its philosophy is treated in the philosophy section.
description: The scripture gathers Choe Je-u's essays, including the Podeongmun, his account of the revelation of 1860 and the worship of the Lord of Heaven, the Nonhangmun, defining Eastern Learning against Western learning, and the 21-character incantation. After his execution in 1864 his successor Choe Si-hyeong, hunted by the authorities, reconstructed the texts, partly from memory, and printed them secretly in 1880. As the scripture of Donghak, it inspired the peasant uprising of 1894; it remains the central scripture of Cheondogyo.
image_caption: Early edition of the Donggyeong daejeon

title: Hymns from Yongdam (Yongdam yusa)
creator: choe-je-u
location: Written at Yongdam, Gyeongju; printed in Danyang, Chungcheong Province
note: Choe Je-u's songs in vernacular Korean script, through which his teaching reached ordinary believers.
description: Alongside his classical Chinese writings, Choe Je-u wrote nine songs in the gasa form in Hangul, intended for peasants and women who could not read Chinese. They describe his search and revelation, praise the Lord of Heaven, exhort followers to sincerity and respect, and announce a coming 'opening' of a new age. Printed by Choe Si-hyeong in 1881, they were sung in Donghak communities and are among the first religious scriptures composed in Korean.
image_caption: Early edition of the Yongdam yusa

title: Principal Book of Won Buddhism (Jeongjeon)
creator: sotaesan
note: Sotaesan's doctrinal book, published just after his death, setting out the Il-won-sang (One Circle) and the practices of Won Buddhism.
description: The Jeongjeon presents the Il-won-sang, the circle symbolising the Dharmakāya Buddha and the original nature of all beings, as the object of faith and model of practice; the 'four graces' of heaven and earth, parents, fellow beings and laws; the 'four essentials' including gender equality and education of others' children; and the three studies of spiritual cultivation, inquiry and choice in action. Published in 1943 under the title Bulgyo jeongjeon, it was revised as part of the Won Buddhist Scriptures (Wonbulgyo gyojeon) of 1962, together with the Daejonggyeong, the sayings of Sotaesan.

title: Essays in Zen Buddhism (First Series)
creator: d-t-suzuki
note: The first of D. T. Suzuki's English books presenting Zen to Western readers as a direct experience of awakening (satori).
description: In this collection, followed by second and third series in 1933 and 1934, Suzuki introduced the history of Chan and Zen, the meaning of satori, the kōan exercise and the Zen monastery, drawing on Chinese sources he was among the first to study, including Dunhuang texts. He presented Zen as the essence of Buddhism and of Eastern spirituality, beyond doctrine and ritual. The books shaped the understanding of Zen among Western intellectuals, artists and the 1950s counterculture. Scholars since the 1980s have questioned his emphasis on experience and his links to nationalist ideas, while recognising his pioneering role. The text is still under copyright.
